papers.title: Wireless millikelvin interconnects for superconducting quantum hardware
papers.abstract: Scalable quantum computing is limited by the dense network of electrical interconnects linking cryogenic quantum processors to room-temperature control electronics. To overcome this bottleneck, considerable effort has focused on cryogenic CMOS electronics and microwave-to-optical transduction, aiming to reduce wiring complexity and thermal loading. Wireless interconnects have recently emerged as a promising complementary approach, yet their compatibility with superconducting quantum hardware remains largely unexplored. Here, we demonstrate the wireless excitation of a superconducting microwave resonator of the type routinely employed for qubit readout, operating at millikelvin temperatures inside a dilution refrigerator. By directly comparing wired and wireless operation within the same cryogenic environment, we show that wireless coupling preserves the intrinsic resonator response while revealing parasitic electromagnetic pathways arising from stray radiation within the cryostat enclosure. These results establish a framework for the co-design of wireless interconnects, cryogenic packaging and superconducting quantum hardware.

summary.summary: This work demonstrates wireless excitation of a superconducting microwave resonator at 20 mK inside a dilution refrigerator, comparing performance against a wired reference at $f_r = 10.8$ GHz using a TX/RX pair with double split-ring resonator metalenses. Direct comparison reveals that wireless excitation preserves intrinsic resonator properties ($Q_i$, $f_r$, temperature-dependent frequency shift from quasiparticles) but exhibits an additional loss channel with $|\Delta Q_L| \approx 650$ arising from stray radiation coupling through unintended pathways within the reflective cryostat cavity.
summary.motivation: Scaling quantum computers to thousands of qubits requires reducing the dense network of interconnects between cryogenic processors and room-temperature electronics, which introduce substantial thermal loading and routing congestion in dilution refrigerators.
summary.method: The authors built a wireless link operating at $\sim$10.6 GHz through a 10 cm diameter aperture between the 4 K and 20 mK stages, using matched TX and RX modules with metalens beam-shaping, and systematically compared wired and wireless excitation of a NbN resonator using cryogenic switches to isolate propagation pathways.
summary.result: At $T_{mxc} = 20$ mK, wireless transmission preserves resonator $Q_i$ and frequency evolution across 20 mK–3 K, but introduces $\approx$650 additional losses in $Q_L$ due to parasitic coupling; RF absorbers suppress cavity reverberation but do not eliminate residual stray excitation with estimated parasitic capacitance $C_p \sim 40$ fF.

papers.title: Phonon down-conversion by normal metals for superconducting devices
papers.abstract: Thanks to low dissipation, superconducting devices are promising for a number of applications, such as detectors and implementations of quantum computation. However, their working can be adversely impacted by quasiparticles, which is why so-called quasiparticle poisoning mechanisms and their mitigation are under intense investigation. Here we focus on one poisoning mechanism, namely pair-breaking phonons, and its mitigation through down-conversion by a normal-metal film - the process in which scattering of high-energy phonons by electrons lowers the energy of the former below the pair-breaking threshold. To study the down-conversion, we introduce a model based on kinetic equations, which we solve both analytically (approximately) and numerically in the steady state. We use the solution the estimate a properly-defined down-conversion efficiency which depends on material parameters (such as the strength of electron-phonon interaction and the phonon transmission coefficient at interfaces) and film and substrate thicknesses. Interestingly, we find that the efficiency is nearly optimal over a finite range of metal thicknesses, with the minimum near-optimal thickness being typically of the order of a micron.

similar_to.title: Phonon downconversion to suppress correlated errors in superconducting qubits

summary.summary: This paper develops a kinetic equation model for phonon down-conversion by normal-metal films, in which high-energy pair-breaking phonons scatter off electrons and lose energy below the qubit gap threshold. The authors solve the coupled equations for electron and phonon distributions in steady state, define a down-conversion efficiency $R_{m qp}$ comparing quasiparticle generation rates with and without the metal, and find that efficiency remains near-optimal ($>90\%$) over a finite metal thickness range with minimum thickness around $0.4\text{–}1\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ for typical parameters.
summary.motivation: Quasiparticle poisoning from high-energy impacts creates correlated error bursts threatening fault tolerance in superconducting qubit arrays; mitigating this requires understanding how normal metals can convert pair-breaking phonons to lower energies before they reach qubits.
summary.method: The authors model a substrate–metal–superconductor stack using kinetic equations for phonon distributions in substrate and metal and electron distribution in metal, incorporating phonon transmission at interfaces ($\eta_{s m}, \eta_{m s}$) and electron-phonon collision integrals parameterized by coupling strengths $\tau_{\mathrm{el}}, \tau_{\mathrm{ph}}$. They solve the steady-state system analytically (deriving equilibrium-like forms) and numerically, using measured/calculated material parameters for Al, Nb, Ti, Cu, Au, Ag, Ta on Si and Al$_2$O$_3$.
summary.result: For monochromatic injection at energy $\Omega_{\mathrm{inj}} > 2\Delta_{\mathrm{Al}} = 0.36\,\mathrm{meV}$, efficiency approaches $98.5\text{–}99\%$ at low injection rate when phonons escape the substrate faster than transmission into the metal ($\tau_{s m} \ll \tau_{\mathrm{es}} \approx 50\,\mu\mathrm{s}$), with Cu/Al/Si achieving highest resilience to increased injection rates; thin metal films fail to suppress the injected peak while thick films heat up, reducing efficiency below peak values near $d_m \sim 1\text{–}10\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ depending on parameters.

papers.title: Transducer leakage error suppression using invariant-based shortcut
papers.abstract: We present a method for suppressing transducer leakage errors in spin-superconducting hybrid quantum systems with the theory of optimal invariant-based shortcut. By mediated virtual photons as a transducer to exchange the energy between the spin qubit and a transmon qubit, the fidelity of the population of the final state features a broad range above 99\% under the influence of leakage error. The leakage probability from computational subspace to non-computational subspace can be effectively suppressed at a lowest value with $0.01$. Based on the optimized pulse control designed by the invariant-based inverse engineering, the high-fidelity quantum iSWAP gate operations and entanglement state preparation within the computational subspace are achieved. {Compared to the traditional $π$ pulse, derivative removal by adiabatic gate, counter-diabatic shortcut schemes, and limited-memory Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno gradient ascent pulse engineering, the optimized shortcut scheme can still achieve a high fidelity with 99\% in the presence of decoherence and control error.} When taking into account the possibility of leakage errors in actual situations, our solution can still largely resist the influence of control errors. The results provides a feasible path for precisely manipulating the quantum state of hybrid quantum systems.

similar_to.title: Heralded Leakage Detection with Preserved Computational-State Coherence in a Fixed-Frequency Transmon

summary.summary: This work presents an invariant-based shortcut (Lewis-Riesenfeld) control scheme to suppress transducer leakage errors in hybrid spin-superconducting quantum systems where a resonator mediates interactions between a GaAs RX spin qubit and a transmon. The optimized pulse protocol achieves iSWAP gate and Bell state preparation with >99% fidelity, reducing leakage probability to 0.01 and demonstrating robustness against decoherence and control errors.
summary.motivation: Hybrid spin-superconducting systems combining long decoherence times of semiconductor spins with fast gates of superconducting qubits suffer from multi-level leakage errors that degrade gate fidelity; a systematic control framework is needed to confine dynamics within the computational subspace.
summary.method: The authors decompose the effective Hamiltonian into computational subspace ($H_\mathrm{sub}$) and leakage ($H_\mathrm{leak}$) contributions, apply Lewis-Riesenfeld invariant theory to design time-dependent Rabi frequency $\Omega(t)$ and detuning $\Delta(t)$ that minimize error sensitivity $q = \eta^2 \sum_k |\int_0^T \langle\psi_0(t)|V(t)|\psi_k(t)\rangle|^2$ via Fourier ansatz with $\nu = 2.27$, and numerically validate against DRAG, counter-diabatic, and LBFGS-GRAPE schemes.
summary.result: The Lewis-Riesenfeld optimized scheme achieves fidelity $>99\%$ for iSWAP operations with leakage probability suppressed to $P_\mathrm{leak} \approx 0.01$ (scaling as $\eta^2$), outperforming $\pi$-pulse and counter-diabatic schemes; Bell state preparation reaches $98\%$ fidelity under simultaneous leakage, decoherence ($T_1^s = 20$ ms, $T_\phi^s = 3$ μs for spin; $T_1^t = T_\phi^t = 60$ μs for transmon), and $±20\%$ control errors with gate time $T = 40$ ns.

papers.title: Precision quantum simulation of magnon spectra and interactions
papers.abstract: Quantum simulation promises to advance materials discovery by accurately simulating complex states of matter, their microscopic excitations, and macroscopic response functions. The central challenge in resolving the underlying interacting dynamics is to combine high-fidelity evolution with the sophisticated control necessary to manipulate individual quasi-particles in quantum many-body states. Here, we report on high-precision simulation of both linear and non-linear response functions in a 2D XY spin-1/2 magnet using an analog-digital superconducting processor of up to 97 qubits. By interleaving digital gates with analog evolution precisely characterized via Hamiltonian learning, we selectively excite magnons at tunable energy densities. Measuring first the linear magnon response -- a central probe in neutron-scattering experiments -- we extract temperature-dependent spectra and lifetimes. Our results reveal stark variations in magnon decay rates across the Brillouin zone, with enhancement near van Hove singularities and suppression for edge-localized modes. Next, we perform a suite of nonlinear measurements, including the study of self-scattering mechanisms, as well as pump-probe spectroscopy to directly characterize the magnon interactions. While matrix-product state simulations capture the dynamics well in either small systems or at low temperatures, their predictions become inaccurate away from these limits. This work demonstrates precise simulation of the interacting dynamics in quantum magnets, and provides key insights into quasi-particles and their microscopic scattering mechanisms.

summary.summary: This work demonstrates high-precision quantum simulation of magnon spectra and interactions in a 2D XY spin-1/2 magnet using a 97-qubit hybrid analog-digital superconducting processor, achieving $g/(2\pi) \approx 9.7$ MHz coupling strength and characterizing both linear and nonlinear magnon response functions with median relative precision of $7 \times 10^{-3}$ in frequency and $7.8 \times 10^{-2}$ in decay rate. The technique combines Hamiltonian learning achieving $4.7 \times 10^{-4}$ per-qubit-per-cycle XEB errors with interleaved digital Z-gate excitation to isolate individual magnon modes, revealing mode-dependent decay rates enhanced near van Hove singularities and suppressed for edge-localized corner modes.
summary.motivation: Precise control over quasi-particle excitations in quantum many-body systems is essential for understanding microscopic scattering mechanisms, yet existing quantum simulators struggle to achieve both high-fidelity state preparation and the local control needed to excite and probe specific modes with tunable energy densities.
summary.method: A global gate protocol (GGP) prepares low-temperature states with controllable energy density in 6 ns, followed by analog evolution under a learned Hamiltonian. Interleaved digital Z-gates with 2 ns switching times excite individual magnon modes, enabling measurement of retarded Green's functions $\chi_\mu(t) = -iA\langle\psi_0|[\hat{b}_\mu(t), \hat{b}_\mu^\dagger(0)]|\psi_0\rangle$. Pump-probe and two-mode collision experiments isolate scattering pathways; MPS simulations fail at elevated temperatures due to volume-law entanglement.
summary.result: Temperature-dependent decay rates $\Gamma \propto (\epsilon - \epsilon_0)^\eta$ with $\eta \approx 0.7$ for high-energy modes reflect self-consistent broadening effects. Corner modes show $\sim 10$ times longer lifetimes than bulk modes; all four corner modes scatter exclusively into each other, forming a decoupled manifold. Nonlinear decay $\alpha_2$ scales as $A^2$ and exhibits negative temperature sensitivity at high energies, distinct from linear decay $\alpha_1$.

papers.title: Deterministic single-electron trapping on solid neon using engineered dielectric surface geometry
papers.abstract: Levitating electron qubit on the surface of solid neon has recently emerged as a promising and intrinsically noise-resilient platform for quantum information processing. Their ultra-clean, inert environment suppresses conventional decoherence pathways associated with lattice disorder, charge traps, and nuclear-spin baths that limit coherence in semiconductor qubits. Yet, uncontrolled surface features such as bumps, valleys, and electrode-defined gaps can bind electrons unintentionally, contributing charge noise and inducing spin-orbit coupling mediated decoherence. To address this challenge, we propose an engineered interface in which a dielectric layer is deposited beneath the solid neon to provide an atomically smooth template, eliminating surface-roughness induced trapping. By selectively etching this dielectric layer at desired qubit locations, deterministic potential minima can be engineered to reliably capture electrons while suppressing unwanted surface bound states. We perform large-scale Schrodinger and Poisson simulation to compare the existing and proposed strategies of electron trapping on neon, obtaining good agreement with recent experimental measurements.

summary.summary: This work develops a three-dimensional Schrödinger–Poisson framework to model electron trapping on solid neon and proposes engineering the dielectric substrate surface to enable deterministic single-electron confinement. The simulations demonstrate that nanoscale surface roughness (bumps and valleys with $\sigma_{\mathrm{rms}} = 3$ nm) substantially perturbs the trapping landscape, but a combination of a planarizing dielectric spacer and selective etching creates controlled potential minima while suppressing parasitic bound states.
summary.motivation: Levitating electrons on solid neon offer long coherence times (approaching 93 μs for charge qubits) and escape conventional decoherence channels, but deterministic electron loading and precise positioning remain unsolved challenges. Unintended trapping by surface roughness, resonator gaps, and substrate features introduces charge noise and decoherence.
summary.method: A three-dimensional Schrödinger–Poisson solver on a $121 \times 121 \times 111$ mesh was used to compute orbital eigenstates and energies for different device geometries: smooth gates, rough surfaces with $\pm 3$ nm perturbations, gates with dielectric spacers of variable thickness $H$, and dielectric with selective etched trenches. The model was validated against experimental orbital splittings of $\Delta E \approx 6.3$–$6.4$ GHz.
summary.result: A continuous dielectric layer (with $\epsilon_r \approx 3.5$) planarizes the surface and eliminates roughness-induced trapping that would shift $\Delta E$ from 6.2 GHz to 10.6 GHz; selective etching of the dielectric recovers $\Delta E \approx 6.1$ GHz while creating deterministic confinement, demonstrating a practical route to scalable, reproducible electron positioning on solid neon.
